intro: Four deep dives for November, one per part, plus hard challenge problems and a language plan. This package was regenerated late in the month after a structure change, so treat it as a menu. Pick one piece, go at your own pace, and let the rest go. Nothing carries over.

items.title: Looped transformers: thinking by running the same layers again
items.why: Looped models reuse the same block several times per token, so depth grows without more weights. This month an open looped MoE model was released and interpretability teams started looking inside. It is a live question whether looping is a real route to better reasoning or just cheaper depth.
items.objective: Explain how a looped transformer differs from a standard one, read the key papers from Universal Transformers to today, and train a tiny looped model that you can run for more loops at test time.
prerequisites: the transformer block (attention, MLP, residual stream)

tasks: Read Universal Transformers, Sec. 1 to 3. Note what is shared across steps and how adaptive halting works
Write 5 sentences: what does weight sharing across depth buy you, and what does it cost?
Read Geiping et al., Sec. 1 to 4. Focus on the prelude, recurrent core and coda design and how they sample the number of loops in training
Read Saunshi et al., Sec. 1 to 3. Write down their claim about looped depth versus chain-of-thought steps
Skim the Ouro paper: how do they train the model to choose how many loops to use?
Read the Goodfire write-up on Inkling 2 Mini and the LessWrong post on interpreting a recurrent LLM. List two ways standard tools like the logit lens need to change for loops
Implement a 2-layer looped transformer in a notebook on a toy task such as addition or parity
Train with a random number of loops, then test with more loops than seen in training. Plot accuracy against loop count

items.continuation: Possible later milestone: adaptive halting, letting the model decide its own loop count. Not scheduled.

items.title: Concentration inequalities, derived from scratch
items.topic: concentration of measure for learning theory
items.why: Every generalization bound, every confidence interval on a benchmark and every random projection argument rests on a few inequalities. Deriving them yourself turns them from facts you recall into tools you can bend.
items.objective: Derive Markov, Chebyshev, Chernoff, Hoeffding and McDiarmid yourself, and use Hoeffding plus a union bound to prove a finite-class generalization bound.

tasks: Read Vershynin HDP, Ch. 1 and Sec. 2.1 to 2.2
Prove Markov and Chebyshev on paper. Then derive the Chernoff bound by applying Markov to exp(tX) and optimizing t
Read Vershynin HDP, Sec. 2.5 to 2.6
Prove Hoeffding's lemma for a bounded variable, then Hoeffding's inequality. Do exercises 2.2.3 and 2.5.5 or the nearest ones in your edition
Read Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, Ch. 2 to 4 (PAC learning and uniform convergence)
Prove that a finite hypothesis class is agnostic PAC learnable with sample size of order log(|H|/delta) / epsilon squared

weeks.focus: Bounded differences and a real use
tasks: Learn McDiarmid's inequality from Vershynin Sec. 2.9 or Shalev-Shwartz Ch. 26
Use Hoeffding to compute how many test questions a benchmark needs to separate two models whose accuracy differs by 2 points

items.title: Statistical mechanics for an ML researcher
items.subject: physics
items.topic: statistical mechanics: entropy, the Boltzmann distribution, free energy
items.why: Softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, the ELBO is a free energy, and diffusion models began as nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Learning the physics properly gives you a second language for generative models and learning dynamics. That is the possible research connection.
items.objective: Understand the microcanonical and canonical ensembles, the partition function and free energy, and the Ising model, then trace each idea into a concrete ML method.

tasks: Read Tong, Statistical Physics, Sec. 1.1 to 1.2 (the microcanonical ensemble)
Watch Susskind Statistical Mechanics lectures 1 to 2
Derive the Boltzmann distribution by maximizing entropy with a fixed mean energy
Read Tong Sec. 1.3 to 1.4
Show that derivatives of log Z give the mean and variance of the energy. Write softmax with a temperature as a Boltzmann distribution
Read Tong Sec. 5.1 to 5.2 (mean field Ising model)
Simulate a 2D Ising model with Metropolis sampling in a notebook and watch the magnetization change near the critical temperature
Read the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics press release on Hopfield and Hinton
Read Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015, Sec. 1 to 2. Write down which physical process their forward diffusion mimics

exercises: Compute Z for a two-level system and plot mean energy against temperature

items.deliverable: A one-page explainer: why your softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, and where free energy shows up in ML. Plus the Ising notebook.
items.definition_of_done: The explainer exists and the Ising simulation shows a visible change around the critical temperature.
items.final_synthesis: Name one ML phenomenon, such as grokking or sudden capability jumps, and argue for or against calling it a phase transition.
items.light_version: Weeks 1 and 2 only: the Boltzmann derivation and the softmax link.
items.continuation: Possible later milestone: energy-based models and Hopfield networks in depth. Not scheduled.

cross_domain.connection: Entropy, temperature and free energy from physics are the same objects as softmax temperature, the ELBO and the noise schedule in diffusion models.

items.title: Conversation craft: better questions and short true stories
items.topic: asking follow-up questions and telling short personal stories
items.why: Good conversations rest on two skills you can practise: asking a real follow-up question and telling a short story with a point. Research finds people who ask more follow-up questions are liked more. Storytellers from The Moth teach a simple, learnable structure.
items.objective: Use follow-up questions on purpose in real conversations, and build a small bank of five short true stories you can tell in under two minutes.

tasks: Read the Harvard summary of Huang et al., It Doesn't Hurt to Ask
In two real conversations, ask at least three follow-up questions before sharing your own view. Notice what changed
Read The Moth, How to Tell a Story, the chapters on finding your story and structure
Listen to three Moth stories and note for each one where it starts, what changes and how it ends
Try Matthew Dicks' Homework for Life: each evening write one sentence about the most story-worthy moment of the day
Pick two moments and shape each into a 90-second story with a clear before and after
Tell one story out loud to a friend or record it for yourself
Ask one open question at the end and listen to the answer fully

challenges.subject: probability
challenges.title: Four random points on a sphere
challenges.question: Choose four points independently and uniformly at random on the surface of a sphere. What is the probability that the tetrahedron they form contains the centre of the sphere?
challenges.tests: Symmetry arguments and clever conditioning in geometric probability
hints: Solve the 2D version first: three points on a circle and a triangle containing the centre.
Fix the lines through the centre and each of three points. Each point can be either end of its line.
Count how many of the 8 sign choices give a tetrahedron that contains the centre.
challenges.solution: 1/8. For each of the first three points, pair it with its antipode. Of the 8 ways to choose ends, exactly one gives a triangle whose cone, with the fourth point, contains the centre.

challenges.subject: maths
challenges.title: A divisibility that forces a square
challenges.question: Let a and b be positive integers such that ab + 1 divides a^2 + b^2. Show that (a^2 + b^2)/(ab + 1) is a perfect square.
challenges.tests: Number theory and the descent method known as Vieta jumping
hints: Set k = (a^2 + b^2)/(ab + 1) and suppose k is not a square.
Among all pairs with this k, take the one with smallest a + b, and view the equation as a quadratic in a.
The other root a' = kb - a = (b^2 - k)/a is a smaller valid solution. Find the contradiction.
challenges.solution: Assume k is not a square and take a minimal solution with a >= b. The other root a' = kb - a is an integer, and a' is positive because k is not a square and a' = 0 would make k = b^2. Also a' < a, which contradicts minimality.

challenges.subject: physics
challenges.title: The curve of fastest descent
challenges.question: A bead slides without friction under gravity from point A to a lower point B that is not directly below A. Which curve joining A and B gives the shortest travel time? Set up the time integral and find the curve.
challenges.tests: Energy conservation and the calculus of variations, or Snell's law by analogy
hints: Speed at depth y is sqrt(2gy) from energy conservation.
Write the time as an integral of ds / v and apply the Euler-Lagrange equation. The integrand does not depend on x, so use the Beltrami identity.
Bernoulli's own trick: treat the bead like light passing through layers with changing speed.
challenges.solution: A cycloid: the curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling circle.

challenges.subject: physics
challenges.title: The Ehrenfest urn and the arrow of time
challenges.question: N balls are split between two urns. Each second one ball, chosen uniformly at random, moves to the other urn. Find the stationary distribution of the number of balls in the left urn. Then find the expected time to return to the state where all balls are in the left urn. Why does this not contradict the second law in practice?
challenges.source: P. and T. Ehrenfest, 1907 urn model
challenges.tests: Markov chains, detailed balance and the meaning of recurrence in statistical mechanics
hints: Guess that each ball is independently in either urn with probability 1/2 and check detailed balance.
For an irreducible chain, the mean return time to state i is 1/pi(i).
Put N = 100 and one move per second into the return time.
challenges.solution: The stationary distribution is Binomial(N, 1/2). The mean return time to all-left is 2^N steps, about 10^30 seconds for N = 100, far longer than the age of the universe.

challenges.subject: chemistry
challenges.title: How stable is benzene?
challenges.question: Hydrogenating cyclohexene to cyclohexane releases about 120 kJ/mol. A model of benzene with three isolated double bonds would release three times that. Measured, benzene releases about 208 kJ/mol. Estimate benzene's extra stability and explain it in terms of electron delocalization.
challenges.source: Northstar original, using standard textbook values
hints: Compute the expected value for three isolated double bonds.
The difference is the stabilization energy.
Think about the six pi electrons spread over the whole ring.
challenges.solution: About 3 x 120 - 208 = 152 kJ/mol of extra stability, from the six pi electrons being delocalized around the ring.

challenges.subject: biology
challenges.title: Do mutations wait for a reason?
challenges.question: Many parallel bacterial cultures are each grown from a few cells and then exposed to a virus. You count resistant colonies in each culture. If resistance were induced by exposure, what would the distribution of counts across cultures look like? What if mutations arose at random during growth, before exposure? Which statistic tells the two apart?
challenges.source: Luria and Delbrueck, Genetics, 1943 (the fluctuation test)
challenges.tests: Mutation theory and the variance of branching processes
hints: Under induction, each cell has the same small chance of becoming resistant at exposure. What distribution is that?
Under random mutation, an early mutation is copied into many descendants.
Compare the variance to the mean.
challenges.solution: Induction gives roughly Poisson counts, so variance is close to the mean. Random prior mutation gives occasional jackpots and variance far above the mean. Luria and Delbrueck saw the jackpots.

challenges.subject: economics
challenges.title: Why used car markets can collapse
challenges.question: Car quality q is uniform on [0, 1] and known only to sellers. A seller values a car at q. A buyer values it at 1.5q but sees only the average quality on sale. Show that at any price p > 0, the market unravels. What does this say about why warranties exist?
challenges.source: Based on Akerlof (1970), The Market for 'Lemons', Quarterly Journal of Economics
hints: At price p, which sellers are willing to sell?
What is the average quality of the cars on offer?
Is the buyer willing to pay p for that average?
challenges.solution: Only sellers with q <= p sell, so average quality is p/2 and buyers value it at 0.75p < p. No positive price clears the market. Warranties and inspections fix this by making quality visible.

challenges.subject: computer_science
challenges.title: Why sorting needs n log n comparisons
challenges.question: Prove that any comparison-based sorting algorithm needs Omega(n log n) comparisons in the worst case.
challenges.source: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms, Sec. 8.1
hints: Model the algorithm as a binary decision tree whose leaves are output orders.
How many leaves must the tree have?
Use log2(n!) and Stirling's approximation.
challenges.solution: The tree needs at least n! leaves, so its height is at least log2(n!), which is Theta(n log n).

challenges.subject: astronomy
challenges.title: How old could a gravity-powered Sun be?
challenges.question: In the 1860s Kelvin argued the Sun shines by slowly contracting. Estimate the Sun's lifetime if its power came only from gravitational energy, roughly G M^2 / R. Use M = 2 x 10^30 kg, R = 7 x 10^8 m and L = 3.8 x 10^26 W. Why did this clash with geology and Darwin, and what resolved it?
challenges.source: Northstar original, based on the Kelvin-Helmholtz timescale
challenges.tests: Order-of-magnitude estimation and the history of stellar physics
hints: Compute G M^2 / R first.
Divide by L to get seconds, then convert to years.
What energy source was unknown before the 20th century?
challenges.solution: About 10^15 s, roughly 30 million years. Geology and evolution needed hundreds of millions of years. Nuclear fusion, understood in the 1920s and 1930s, resolved it.

challenges.subject: philosophy
challenges.title: Newcomb's problem
challenges.question: A predictor who is almost always right sets out two boxes. Box A is clear and holds 1,000. Box B holds 1,000,000 if the predictor foresaw that you would take only box B, and nothing otherwise. You may take box B alone or both boxes. Give the strongest argument for each choice, and say which principle of rational choice each argument relies on.
challenges.source: Robert Nozick, Newcomb's Problem and Two Principles of Choice, 1969
challenges.tests: Decision theory: expected utility versus dominance, causal versus evidential reasoning
hints: Write the expected payoff of each choice given the predictor's accuracy.
Now argue that the boxes are already filled. Whatever is in them, taking both gives 1,000 more.
Ask whether your choice causes the contents or only gives evidence about them.
challenges.solution: There is no agreed answer. One-boxers use evidential expected utility. Two-boxers use dominance and causal decision theory. The value is in seeing exactly where the two principles split.
